clue.text: Nearly go out and ask for the sun?

parts.note: a candle flame gutters when it flickers and is on the point of going out
to press for something is to urge or demand it

explanation.surface: A dying fire seems to be begging the sun to come out and help.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sun is a British tabloid newspaper, an example of the sensational popular papers; the question mark flags the definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sun is a well-known British tabloid, an example of the sensational downmarket newspapers.

parts.note: read as a comparative, someone whose interest lies more with the stomach, that is a lover of fine food and eating well

explanation.surface: Someone who cares more about their belly than anything else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'More concerned with gut' reads like a person driven by instinct, but it is a person devoted to the pleasures of the stomach.
explanation.definitionFit: A connoisseur of good food is a person whose chief concern is what goes into the stomach.

indicators.note: the starting letter of the maths word is placed inside the word for the college

parts.note: a tech is a technical college

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter only

explanation.surface: Beginning a maths course at a technical college.
explanation.walkthrough: TECH is short for technical college, a British further-education institution; the whole clue also describes what a lecturer does.
explanation.definitionFit: Instructing students, getting them started on sums at a college, is what a lecturer or tutor does.

clue.text: Deem 'Reg' wrong to have come out

indicators.note: the letters of the two words are put wrong, that is rearranged

explanation.surface: A man called Reg is judged mistaken for having revealed himself.
explanation.definitionFit: Having come out is having appeared or surfaced, the past participle of a verb of appearing.

clue.text: Dogged us dupe stupidly embracing right

indicators.note: the rearranged letters hug or enclose the abbreviation for right
the words us dupe are treated stupidly, jumbled into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone stubbornly fooled us, grabbing a right-wing cause along the way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dogged' looks like the adjective meaning stubborn, but it is the past tense of the verb to dog, follow closely.
explanation.definitionFit: To be dogged is to be followed or hounded persistently, i.e. chased.

clue.text: Acquit former copper with large head

parts.note: ex means former, as in ex-wife
Cu is the chemical symbol for copper
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large
pate is an old word for the head, especially its crown

explanation.surface: A court clears an ex-policeman with a big head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' suggests a policeman but gives the chemical symbol CU.
explanation.definitionFit: To acquit someone is to clear them of blame, the meaning of the Latin-based verb used here.

definitions.meaning: a spot is a location or scene, as the backdrop where a story takes place
a setter composing a crossword is engaged in compiling it, the setter's own word for that work

explanation.definitionFit: A setting is a place or backdrop; setting is also what a crossword setter does when composing a puzzle.

indicators.note: the end letters of the country go inside the word for dirty

parts.note: crude means dirty or vulgar

indicators.note: the ends of a word are its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A dirty political campaign ends up in Serbia.
explanation.definitionFit: A crusade is a vigorous campaign for a cause, from the medieval holy wars.

clue.text: View the French held in disdain by English

indicators.note: the French article is held inside the word for disdain

parts.note: contempt is scorn or disdain
la is the feminine form of 'the' in French

explanation.surface: The English look down on the French with disdain.
explanation.definitionFit: To view something thoughtfully is to consider or ponder it, a verb sense.

indicators.note: playing suggests the letters are played about with, rearranged
not tells us to leave out the letter for new

parts.note: the instrument's name, taken as written

explanation.surface: A concert performance featuring a clarinet that is not new.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not new' removes N from CLARINET, leaving CLARIET; 'playing' rearranges those letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A recital is a musical performance, often by a soloist.

clue.text: Superficial labour leader hit with egg, possibly

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its opening letter
possibly signals the letters could be arranged otherwise

explanation.surface: The Labour Party leader is hit with an egg in a shallow stunt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Labour leader' suggests a politician, but it gives only L; 'possibly' rearranges HITWITHEGG.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone lacking depth or substance is trivial, unimportant, of little weight.

parts.note: mph, miles per hour, is a measure of speed

explanation.surface: A fast-moving seductress in New York.
explanation.definitionFit: Both a siren and a nymph are mythical beautiful female spirits, and nymph can mean an alluring young woman.

indicators.note: the porridge word comes before the fish word

parts.note: gruel is a thin porridge
ling is a long-bodied sea fish of the cod family

explanation.surface: An exhausting meal of porridge followed by fish.
explanation.definitionFit: Something trying is exhausting and taxing.

clue.text: Got into dodgy trend taking double ecstasy

indicators.note: dodgy means unreliable or out of order, so the letters are rearranged
double means the ecstasy letter is taken twice over

parts.note: E is slang for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: Someone got into a shady drug scene taking a double dose of ecstasy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taking' adds two Es to TREND before 'dodgy' rearranges the lot.
explanation.definitionFit: To have got into a place is to have gone in, the past tense of a verb of going inside.

parts.note: reads as having another go as a precaution, but means a court hearing a legal case again

explanation.surface: Having another go, just to be safe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'just in case' looks like 'as a precaution', but 'just' hints at justice and 'case' at a lawsuit.
explanation.definitionFit: A second trial of a lawsuit in court is a fresh hearing of that case.

definitions.meaning: a single swallow or gulp of liquid
... beer is beer drawn from a cask rather than a bottle

explanation.definitionFit: A gulp of liquid is a draught, and beer served from the cask is also called draught.

indicators.note: the supplier word carries the abbreviation for little inside it

parts.note: a pusher is someone who sells illegal drugs
L is short for little, as in L-plate or small sizes

explanation.surface: A slicker drug dealer carrying a small amount.
explanation.definitionFit: Plush means luxurious or posh, so more plush is more stylish and expensive-looking.

indicators.note: say tells us the word is spoken, giving a single letter that sounds like it

parts.note: the letter U sounds like the word you
top means leading or foremost
Ian is a typical Scottish man's name

explanation.surface: A leading Scotsman tells you his notion of perfection.
explanation.walkthrough: Ian is the Scottish form of John, so crosswords use it for any Scotsman.
explanation.definitionFit: Ideal in the sense of perfect but impractical, as in an imagined perfect society.

indicators.note: the tear word takes the train word inside it

parts.note: a rent is a tear or rip in cloth
to train a gun on a target is to aim it

explanation.surface: Clothes suffer wear and tear while travelling by train.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wear and tear' reads as one phrase, but 'Wear' alone is the definition and 'and' a link; 'train' is a verb, to point.
explanation.definitionFit: Raiment is an old word for clothing, what one wears.

clue.text: Dispose of them, commonly in box

indicators.note: the clipped pronoun sits inside the box word

parts.note: a crate is a wooden box
in common or casual speech, them is shortened to 'em

explanation.surface: Get rid of them, usually by putting them in a box.
explanation.definitionFit: To burn a corpse to ashes is one way to dispose of the dead.

indicators.note: the criminal word comes before the evidence word

parts.note: a con is a convict, a criminal
a sign is an indication or piece of evidence

explanation.surface: Lock up a criminal before the evidence comes out.
explanation.definitionFit: To put something away for safekeeping or disposal is to hand it over or deliver it.

indicators.note: the word it is set inside the stone, like a gem in a mount

parts.note: agate is a banded semi-precious stone
it, with the 's as a link

explanation.surface: This is engraved in stone as fact.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rock' looks like a stone, echoing 'stone', but it is the verb to shake or disturb.
explanation.definitionFit: To rock is to shake or disturb, as a scandal stirs people up.

indicators.note: the helping word comes after the trouble word

parts.note: ado is fuss or trouble, as in much ado
a ration is a portion or helping

explanation.surface: Love comes once help arrives after trouble.
explanation.definitionFit: Adoration is deep love or worship.

parts.note: a wing is a faction of a party, as the left wing

explanation.surface: A small group in the party does an about-face.
explanation.definitionFit: A swing is a change of direction or opinion, as a reversal in voters' support.

indicators.note: the pious word is placed in the word for the main

parts.note: the main is a poetic term for the open sea
pi is short for pious, sanctimonious

explanation.surface: A self-righteous man named Brown is out at sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brown' looks like a person, but it is the colour.
explanation.definitionFit: A reddish-brown pigment from cuttlefish ink is the colour of old photographs.

clue.text: Plastered if I cement inside building

indicators.note: the letters are found inside the run of words

explanation.surface: Plasterwork goes on if I put cement inside a building.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plastered' could be an anagram indicator for IF I CEMENT, but the letter count kills that.
explanation.definitionFit: An edifice is a large, imposing building.

parts.note: the setter refers to himself, so setter's is I'm, I am

indicators.note: the wheeze word traps the beginner's letter inside

parts.note: to pant is to breathe heavily, wheeze
L is a learner, a beginner, as on L-plates

explanation.surface: The setter's clever scheme catches a novice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wheeze' suggests a clever trick, but it is the verb, to breathe with difficulty.
explanation.definitionFit: To implant is to fix firmly in place, embed.

indicators.note: smashing means breaking apart, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A gentleman calls out to a wonderful bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smashing' reads as British slang for wonderful, describing the bird, but is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A small brown songbird famous for its night-time song.
